introduction: The first prayers here ask something unusual: that the oppressor be transformed, strangers made friends, and “the throne of tyranny” replaced with “the seat of justice”. Others cry out on behalf of the persecuted, ask that kings and the learned be guided to equity, and commit the unrepentant to God. The Hebrew prophets are the great voices of prayer for justice: Amos’s “let judgment run down as waters”, Habakkuk’s “how long shall I cry”, Isaiah’s “relieve the oppressed”, the Psalmist’s prayer for the king. Saul’s conversion is the classic case of a persecutor changed, and “Father, forgive them” the classic prayer for one. The imprecatory Psalm, “break their teeth”, is the kind of prayer these mostly decline to pray; and Jonah, angry that his enemies were spared, asks whether those who pray for an oppressor’s change of heart really want it.
questions: Reading 2 asks that the oppressor be transformed. Why is that harder to pray than a prayer for his removal?
Compare the Psalmist’s “break their teeth” with reading 24’s “deal with them as beseemeth Thee”. What is each praying for?
Several prayers are for rulers. What can prayer for those in power accomplish, and what must accompany it?
Jonah resented God’s mercy to Nineveh. What would it cost the persecuted for these prayers to be answered?

outside.why: “Thou seest what hath befallen Thy chosen ones at the hands of the oppressors.” The souls under the altar: how long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge?
A prayer to transform the oppressor. The persecutor Saul on the Damascus road: suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven; Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
And the prayer made for executioners while they worked: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
“Make strangers into friends.” Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity will become as though he was a bosom friend.
Protect Thy weak servants from the tyranny of the cruel. Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
Thou seest the oppressed among the wicked. O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!
By the sighing of the hearts of the oppressed. I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and have heard their cry.
The Wronged One between the fangs of wolves. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Enable princes and the learned to execute justice. Give the king thy judgments, O God; he shall judge the poor of the people, and shall break in pieces the oppressor.
Replace the throne of tyranny with the seat of justice. Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Illumine the horizon of Thy justice. I will restore thy judges as at the first; afterward thou shalt be called, The city of righteousness.
Aid the kings of the earth to walk in guidance and justice. Paul asks prayers for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life.
The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
May you be aided to show justice and fairness. What doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy?
Adorn Thy servants with truthfulness and their rulers with justice. Seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Pray that God may guide these foolish ones. Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.
Be fair in the Cause of God. Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or parents or kindred.

“Deal with their first and their last and their liars as beseemeth Thee.” The Psalmist is less restrained: break their teeth, O God, in their mouth. The guide’s prayers ask chiefly that oppressors be changed, and leave judgement to God. What is the difference between that and the Psalmist’s cry, and is there a place for his?
Avenge not yourselves: vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Jonah prayed for justice on Nineveh and was angry when it repented and was spared. Would those who pray reading 2 be content if it were answered?

shortfall: Readings 11 to 13, 16, 17 and 21 to 23 repeat the petition for justice by different Names of God and were left with their neighbours’ companions.
